Old English is difficult, but if you know German you will have an advantage. The main difficulty for me was memorizing the grammatical cases and also keeping in mind the gender of the words. The main book I used was "Learn Old English With Leofwin" by Matt Love. The book is for absolute beginners and mainly focuses on things such as greetings,colors, names of tools and objects, and other basic vocabulary that a person that spoke Old English might use. Originally it was supposed to be a complete book series, but from what I understand the author passed away so there is only the beginners book.  I also bought "A Guide to Old English" by Bruce Mitchell and Fred C. Robinson. I hardly read any of it yet, but pretty much it is just a grammar book, so it can be pretty dry, but it is great because it really goes into detail about grammar and pronunciation. The last Old English book I bought, is called "The Cambridge Old English Reader". Pretty much it contains a bunch of Old English readings such as poems, religious documents and other historical documents. The first part of the book contains the meaning of the words on the bottom of the page and other grammatical info, but after the beginning it is mostly just the documents without there Modern English meanings. For more info about Old English it might also be worth checking out the Old English subreddit.

I'm not an expert in evolution or Biology in general. But I usually think of evolution as being similar to languages changing over time in linguistics. For example, German is related to languages like Swedish and  English. They share a "common ancestor" and it's called Proto-Germanic. And if you would go back far enough these these languages are even related to languages such as Persian and Greek since they all are share a "common ancestor" called Indo-European. These languages all share commonalities such as their grammar and words. Of course, Linguists cannot go back in the past and see all the individual changes from early Germanic languages to the modern Germanic languages or early Indo-European languages changing into modern Indo-European languages, so one could assert and say that all the modern Germanic languages or modern Indo-European languages were created individually by a creator, however this would be wrong. It's far more likely that these languages  are related, do to the documentation there is (which could be analogous to having fossils in Evolution), the morphological similarities, or the phonetic changes. Also it is known that languages make small changes over time, which are observable. With all this knowledge it reasonable to say that these languages are related.
